summary: Describes the format and publication mechanisms IANA uses to distribute the DNSSEC trust anchors for the root zone, which clients need to validate DNSSEC answers. It obsoletes RFC 7958.

eli5.summary: To check that DNS answers are genuine, you need a starting point you already trust. This explains where to get the official one. It replaces RFC 7958.

subtitle: How IANA publishes the DNSSEC trust anchors for the DNS root zone, as an XML file with signed delivery options.

tldr.problem: A client that wants to validate DNSSEC answers from the root zone needs a trust anchor, and needs a well-defined way to get and check it.
tldr.mechanism: IANA publishes the root zone trust anchors as an XML document of key digests (and optionally the keys), fetched over HTTPS or HTTP, with a detached CMS signature and TLS as ways to check origin.
tldr.outcome: This document obsoletes RFC 7958. It drops the PGP and certificate-request methods, adds optional public key information, and adds security guidance for relying parties.

facts.label: Format
facts.value: XML, defined with RELAX NG Compact

today: RFC 9718 is an Informational document that obsoletes RFC 7958, and it has not been obsoleted or updated in the unit metadata. It is the current description of how IANA publishes the root zone trust anchors.

sections.title: Why Trust Anchors Are Needed
sections.content:
DNSSEC signs DNS data. A response carries signatures that let a client check the integrity and authenticity of a record set by following a chain of signatures to a trust anchor. Why you trust the anchor is outside the DNSSEC protocol, but at least one anchor is required for DNSSEC to work.

Publishing the root zone trust anchors is an IANA function performed by ICANN through its affiliate Public Technical Identifiers (PTI). Other organizations might use different formats, but the RFC says most operators and software vendors have chosen to rely on the IANA trust anchors.

The formats here complement RFC 5011, which handles secure in-band succession of trust anchors once trust exists. This document describes one way to establish the initial anchor that RFC 5011 can then maintain. The RFC also notes that its formats do not match the RFC 4033 definition of a trust anchor (a configured DNSKEY or DS hash), but a system can convert the IANA material into a DS record.
sections.eli5: Checking a signature needs a starting point you trust without proof, like the first stamp you believe in. This document says where to get the official one for the top of the DNS.

sections.title: The XML Trust Anchor File
sections.content:
IANA publishes the trust anchors as an XML document that holds the hashes of the DNSKEY records and, optionally, the keys. The syntax is given in RELAX NG Compact form. The hashes are mandatory and consistent with the presentation format of a DS record; the keys and flags are optional and consistent with the presentation format of a DNSKEY record.

The TrustAnchor element wraps everything. Its id is an opaque string, its source is advisory and likely a URL, and its Zone element names the zone, with the root zone written as a single period. It holds one or more KeyDigest elements.

Each KeyDigest stands for a past, current or potential future DNSKEY. It has an id, a validFrom attribute and an optional validUntil attribute that give the time range in which it can be used as a trust anchor. Its child elements are KeyTag, Algorithm, DigestType and Digest. An optional publickeyinfo pattern adds PublicKey and Flags, which is useful when IANA has an anchor not yet published in the DNS root and for checking against the Digest.

The file can contain XML comments, but they are only human-readable commentary, not extensions.
sections.eli5: The file is a list. Each entry is a fingerprint of a master key, plus dates saying when it is okay to use it, and sometimes the key itself.

sections.title: A Worked Example
sections.content:
The RFC gives an example file with three KeyDigest entries: key tag 19036 with a validUntil in the past, key tag 20326 with its full public key and Flags of 257, and key tag 38696 (labelled in a comment as "KSK-2024") with a digest only. All use algorithm 8 and digest type 2.

From it, the RFC derives a DS record set with two records, for key tags 20326 and 38696. The 19036 entry is excluded because its validUntil has passed. The DNSKEY record set has only one record, for key tag 20326, because the 38696 entry has no publickeyinfo, so its DNSKEY cannot be calculated.
sections.eli5: The example shows that an old key with an expired date gets skipped, and that you can only rebuild a full key when the file included it.

sections.title: Retrieval and Accepting Trust Anchors
sections.content:
The XML document is available over HTTPS and HTTP at data.iana.org/root-anchors/root-anchors.xml. Validator operators may accept or reject the anchors under any policy they choose.

To help check content and origin, IANA offers two aids. One is a detached Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) signature, root-anchors.p7s, that chains to an ICANN-controlled Certificate Authority (CA); it helps operators who got the ICANN CA public key through a trusted out-of-band route. The other is TLS: if a system trusts the CA used for data.iana.org, HTTPS SHOULD be used instead of HTTP to gain assurance of data origin. The ICANN CA is not itself a DNSSEC trust anchor, only an optional verification mechanism.

The older PGP-signed message and self-issued certificate signing request from RFC 7958 are removed, because they relied on a trust model that mixed out-of-band trust of authentication keys with out-of-band trust of the DNSSEC root keys. Assurance now comes from the Web PKI or the ICANN CA, bolstered by informal comparisons by users such as software vendors.
sections.eli5: You can download the list from IANA's website. To make sure nobody swapped it, you can check a signature or make sure the website connection is secure.

sections.title: Security Considerations for Relying Parties
sections.content:
The body of the RFC does not set required behavior for relying parties, but the file's contents need care.

  • validUntil. It is optional. A party using a KeyDigest without it can switch to one that has it, as long as the date is in the future and the KeyTag, Algorithm, DigestType and Digest match. Relying parties SHOULD NOT use a KeyDigest outside its validFrom and validUntil range.
  • Digest versus publickeyinfo. If a Digest would not be a proper DS record for the key in publickeyinfo, relying parties MUST NOT use that KeyDigest. The same anchor can change its Digest and KeyTag between file versions, for example when a key is revoked, so matching must be implemented carefully.
  • Different outputs. Parties that require publickeyinfo will store fewer anchors than those that need only a Digest, so two systems can end up with different sets.
sections.eli5: Only use a key during the dates listed, and if a fingerprint does not match its key, throw that entry away.

sections.title: What IANA Must Do
sections.content:
Each time IANA produces a new trust anchor it MUST publish it in this format. IANA MAY delay publication for operational reasons, such as having a new key in multiple facilities. When a published anchor is no longer suitable, IANA MUST set a validUntil date for it, which MAY be in the past or the future.

The identifier id-mod-dns-resource-record (value 70) that RFC 7958 added to the "SMI Security for PKIX Module Identifier" registry is not used by this document. Appendix B records the history of the first two root Key Signing Keys, including first publication of the first trust anchor on 2010-07-15.
sections.eli5: IANA promises to post every new master key in this format and to mark old ones with an end date.
